justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-sloping trajectory from a baseline around 2020, with each successive horizon incorporating a small positive drift. For the one-day estimate, I anchored near the prevailing level and applied minimal adjustment, as short-term mean reversion tends to dominate. For the one-week estimate, I factored in a slight trend continuation, likely reflecting a backdrop of stable or gradually improving macro conditions at the time. The one-month estimate extends that drift further, reaching roughly 2060, consistent with a slow grind higher that many medium-term models suggest when volatility is moderate and no major catalyst is imminent.

The confidence interval widths expand substantially as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the compounding of daily uncertainty over time. At one day, the 70-point spread is relatively tight, consistent with typical intraday-to-next-day realized volatility in equity index territory. By one week, the spread widens to roughly 290 points, and at one month it reaches 620 points, reflecting the well-known square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty plus additional uncertainty about regime changes, earnings cycles, or macro surprises that become more probable over longer windows.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include sudden geopolitical shocks, an unexpected central bank policy pivot, or a credit event in a systemically important institution — any of which could produce gap moves that exceed the tails I specified. On the upside, a surprise resolution of a major geopolitical conflict, a stronger-than-expected economic data release, or a significant policy stimulus announcement could push prices well above the upper bound of the one-month interval.

It is also worth acknowledging that my intervals were constructed with implicit assumptions about a roughly normal distribution of returns and relatively stable volatility. If realized volatility were to spike — as it does in crisis episodes — the true distribution would have much fatter tails than my intervals suggest, meaning the stated 90% confidence intervals would undercover actual outcomes more often than intended. These tail events are structurally difficult to capture in point-in-time probabilistic forecasts.
